Aula 01 -- Pre-class

Diagnostic + Who Is Fabiana? -- Mapping Your English

Supply chain vocabulary audit and diagnostic elicitation. Key words: supply chain, vendor, procurement, stakeholder, compliance, logistics, milestone, forecast, shipment, delivery, leverage, deployment. Structures: present simple, present perfect, past simple.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Supply chain -- the entire system of producing and delivering a product
"We need to optimize our supply chain to reduce costs." (Cadeia de suprimentos)
Vendor -- a company or person that sells goods or services
"Our main vendor is based in Singapore." (Fornecedor)
Procurement -- the process of finding and buying goods for a company
"The procurement team handles all equipment purchases." (Aquisição)
Stakeholder -- a person with an interest or concern in a project
"We briefed all stakeholders before the meeting." (Parte interessada)
Compliance -- following rules, regulations, or standards
"All vendors must meet our compliance requirements." (Conformidade)
Logistics -- the detailed coordination of a complex operation
"The logistics of the rollout were challenging." (Logística)
Milestone -- a significant event or achievement in a project
"Reaching Q3 targets was a major milestone." (Marco)
Forecast -- a prediction of future trends based on data
"The demand forecast looks strong for next quarter." (Previsão)
Shipment -- goods sent from one place to another
"The shipment arrived two days late." (Remessa)
Delivery -- the act of bringing goods to a destination
"We expect delivery by the end of the month." (Entrega)
Leverage -- to use something to maximum advantage
"We can leverage our relationship with the vendor." (Alavancar)
Deployment -- the process of putting resources into use
"The terminal deployment is scheduled for October." (Implantação)

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

Fabiana works in the supply chain department at Bloomberg. Every day, she coordinates with vendors and manages procurement for specialized trading equipment. Last quarter, her team handled a critical shipment delay when a logistics partner failed to meet compliance standards. "We have dealt with similar situations before," she explains. "The key is having a solid forecast and keeping all stakeholders informed. I have worked at Bloomberg for several years, and every milestone we reach teaches us something about leveraging our vendor relationships for better delivery outcomes."

1. Which tense does Fabiana use to describe her daily routine?
A Present simple: "works", "coordinates", "manages"
B Present perfect: "has worked", "has coordinated"
C Past simple: "worked", "coordinated"
2. Which tense describes the shipment delay as a completed past event?
A Present perfect: "have handled"
B Past simple: "handled", "failed"
C Present simple: "handles", "fails"
3. Why does Fabiana say "We have dealt with similar situations" using the present perfect?
A Because it happened at a specific time last year.
B Because it is happening right now.
C Because the experience connects past actions to the present moment.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Tense Review (B2 Diagnostic)

GRAMMAR

Revisão dos 3 tempos verbais presentes no texto. / Review of the 3 tenses found in the text.

Tense / TempoUse / UsoExample / Exemplo
Present SimpleRotinas, fatos permanentes / Routines, permanent factsFabiana works in supply chain.
Past SimpleAções completas no passado / Completed past actionsHer team handled a delay last quarter.
Present PerfectExperiência acumulada, conexão passado-presente / Accumulated experienceWe have dealt with similar situations.
Key difference / Diferença-chavePast simple = QUANDO importa ("last quarter"). Present perfect = a EXPERIÊNCIA importa ("before", "for years").

First Contact -- Introducing Yourself to International Suppliers

Third conditional in supply chain contexts. New vocabulary: lead time, purchase order, freight, sourcing, invoice, end-to-end, turnaround, carrier, clearance, allocation. Expressions: carry out, look into, put forward.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Lead time -- the time between placing an order and receiving it
"The lead time for this component is four weeks." (Prazo de entrega)
Purchase order -- a formal document requesting goods from a supplier
"We submitted the purchase order yesterday." (Ordem de compra)
Freight -- goods transported by truck, ship, or plane; also the cost of transport
"The freight cost was lower than expected." (Frete)
Sourcing -- the process of finding suppliers for goods or services
"We are sourcing new vendors for the APAC region." (Fornecimento)
Invoice -- a document showing what you owe for goods or services
"Please send the invoice to our finance department." (Fatura)
End-to-end -- covering the entire process from start to finish
"We offer an end-to-end supply chain solution." (Ponta a ponta)
Turnaround -- the time needed to complete a task or process
"They promised a two-week turnaround on repairs." (Tempo de resposta)
Carrier -- a company that transports goods
"Our carrier confirmed the delivery date." (Transportadora)
Clearance -- official permission for goods to pass through customs
"Customs clearance took longer than expected." (Desembaraço)
Allocation -- the distribution of resources or products to different areas
"The allocation of terminals to each office is decided quarterly." (Alocação)

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

Last month, Bloomberg received a purchase order from a new client in Tokyo. The lead time was tight, and the carrier could not guarantee clearance before the deadline. Fabiana's team had to find an alternative sourcing strategy. "If we had started the procurement process earlier, we would have avoided the delay," Fabiana explained. "And if the vendor had sent the invoice on time, we would not have missed the freight window." In the end, the team managed to carry out a fast turnaround by leveraging their end-to-end contract with a backup supplier. The allocation was adjusted, and the shipment arrived just two days late.

1. What structure does Fabiana use to talk about a past situation that did NOT happen?
A "If we start earlier, we will avoid the delay."
B "If we had started earlier, we would have avoided the delay."
C "If we started earlier, we would avoid the delay."
2. Why does the third conditional use "had + past participle" in the if-clause?
A Because the action is happening now.
B Because it refers to an unreal past situation that cannot be changed.
C Because it describes a future plan.
3. What does "carry out" mean in "carry out a fast turnaround"?
A To execute or complete a task.
B To transport goods outside.
C To cancel a process.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Third Conditional

GRAMMAR

Usado para falar de situações irreais no passado. / Used to talk about unreal past situations.

Form / FormaStructure / EstruturaExample / Exemplo
Affirmative / AfirmativaIf + had + past participle, would have + past participleIf we had started earlier, we would have avoided the delay.
Negative / NegativaIf + had not + past participle, would not have + past participleIf the vendor had not sent the invoice late, we would not have missed the deadline.
Question / PerguntaWould + subject + have + past participle if + had + past participle?Would you have chosen a different carrier if you had known the freight cost?
Key point / Ponto-chaveO third conditional fala de um passado IRREAL. Não aconteceu. Serve para refletir: "O que TERIA acontecido se..."

Aula 03 -- Pre-class

When Things Go Wrong -- Handling Delays and Escalations

Modal perfects in supply chain crisis contexts. New vocabulary: escalation, bottleneck, backlog, disruption, contingency, expedite, deadline, inventory, penalty, oversight. Expressions: bring about, account for, phase out.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Escalation -- raising an issue to a higher level of authority
"The escalation reached the VP within hours." (Escalonamento)
Bottleneck -- a narrow point that slows down the entire process
"The bottleneck is in the documentation process." (Gargalo)
Backlog -- an accumulation of unfinished work or orders
"We have a backlog of thirty units at the port." (Acumulado)
Disruption -- a major interruption to the normal flow of operations
"The disruption affected all APAC deliveries." (Ruptura)
Contingency -- a backup plan in case the main plan fails
"We need a contingency plan for this route." (Contingência)
Expedite -- to speed up a process or make it happen faster
"Can we expedite the customs clearance?" (Agilizar)
Deadline -- the final date by which something must be completed
"The deadline for clearance is Thursday." (Prazo final)
Inventory -- the stock of goods available for sale or distribution
"Inventory is running low at the Tokyo office." (Estoque)
Penalty -- a financial punishment for breaking rules or missing deadlines
"We will face a penalty from the client." (Penalidade)
Oversight -- a mistake caused by not paying enough attention
"The oversight in compliance caused the delay." (Descuido)

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

Last week, a major disruption hit the APAC terminal shipment. The carrier should have confirmed the customs clearance on Friday, but they did not. As a result, a backlog of thirty units is now sitting at the port. The bottleneck was caused by an oversight in the documentation process — the logistics team must have missed the updated compliance requirements. Fabiana believes the escalation might have been avoided if they had implemented a contingency plan earlier. Now the team is working to expedite the process before the deadline on Thursday, or they will face a penalty from the client. The inventory at the Tokyo office is running critically low.

1. What structure does the text use to criticize the carrier for NOT confirming?
A "should have confirmed" -- the right thing that did NOT happen
B "must have confirmed" -- a strong deduction
C "might have confirmed" -- a possibility
2. Why does the text say "must have missed" about the logistics team?
A Because they are criticizing the team.
B Because they are making a strong deduction about what probably happened.
C Because they are not sure at all.
3. What does "might have been avoided" express?
A Certainty that it was avoided.
B Criticism of someone who did not avoid it.
C A possibility -- maybe it could have been avoided, maybe not.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Modal Perfects

GRAMMAR

Modal + have + past participle = falar sobre o passado com diferentes significados. / Modal + have + past participle = talk about the past with different meanings.

Modal PerfectMeaning / SignificadoExample / Exemplo
should have + ppO certo que NÃO aconteceu (crítica/arrependimento) / The right thing that did NOT happenWe should have flagged this earlier.
must have + ppDedução forte sobre o passado / Strong deduction about the pastThey must have missed the deadline.
might have + ppPossibilidade (talvez tenha acontecido) / Possibility about the pastThe disruption might have been avoided.
Ponto-chave / Key pointTodos usam modal + HAVE + past participle. A diferença está no SIGNIFICADO: should = crítica, must = certeza, might = possibilidade.

Navigating Hierarchy -- Communicating Across Levels

WISH + past simple / past perfect (I wish I knew..., I wish I had known...) for expressing regret. New vocabulary: hierarchy, counterpart, align, bandwidth, chain of command, peer, subordinate, delegate, oversight, rapport, liaison, mandate, buy-in. Expressions: report to, loop in, touch base.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Hierarchy -- the levels of authority in an organization
"Understanding the hierarchy tells you who decides what." (Hierarquia)
Counterpart -- a person with the same role in another team
"Klaus is my counterpart on the supplier side." (Contraparte)
Align -- to bring people or plans into agreement
"We need to align with the director before we act." (Alinhar)
Bandwidth -- the time and energy you have for more work
"I don't have the bandwidth to lead another project." (Disponibilidade)
Chain of command -- the order of authority decisions flow through
"Follow the chain of command before you escalate." (Cadeia de comando)
Peer -- a colleague at the same level as you
"I discussed the issue with a peer in logistics." (Colega de mesmo nível)
Subordinate -- a person who works under your authority
"A good manager supports every subordinate." (Subordinado)
Delegate -- to give a task or responsibility to someone
"I will delegate the report to my analyst." (Delegar)
Oversight -- responsibility for supervising work
"The director has oversight of all APAC accounts." (Supervisão)
Rapport -- a relationship of trust and easy communication
"She built strong rapport with the whole team." (Sintonia)
Liaison -- a person who connects two teams
"Maria is our liaison with their logistics team." (Elo de ligação)
Mandate -- the official authority to decide or act
"He has no mandate to approve large discounts." (Mandato)
Buy-in -- agreement and support from the people involved
"We need buy-in from senior management first." (Adesão)

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

After the Munich delay, Fabiana decided to map TechFlow's hierarchy. Klaus, her counterpart, explained that the operations director holds full oversight and the final mandate. Looking back, Fabiana said: "I wish I had known the chain of command from the start." She also admitted: "I wish I knew the director personally." To move faster, she chose to align with Klaus first, build rapport with his peer Anna, and ask Klaus to delegate routine tasks to his subordinates. Because Klaus needs buy-in from the director for any credit, Maria will act as the liaison and Fabiana will free up some bandwidth to lead the next review.

1. Which sentence expresses regret about a PAST situation?
A "I wish I know the chain of command."
B "I wish I had known the chain of command from the start."
C "I wish I will know the chain of command."
2. What does "I wish I knew the director personally" mean?
A She does not know the director now, and regrets it.
B She knew the director in the past.
C She will meet the director tomorrow.
3. Why does Klaus need buy-in from the director?
A Because the director has oversight and the final mandate for credits.
B Because the director is his subordinate.
C Because Anna is the liaison for freight.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- WISH

GRAMMAR

Usado para expressar arrependimento ou desejo de mudança. / Used to express regret or a desire for change.

Form / FormaMeaning / SentidoExample / Exemplo
wish + past simpleArrependimento sobre o presente / Regret about nowI wish I knew who my counterpart is.
wish + past perfectArrependimento sobre o passado / Regret about the pastI wish I had aligned with the director sooner.
wish + wouldIncomodo com o comportamento de alguém / Annoyance with behaviorI wish they would respect the chain of command.
Key point / Ponto-chaveApós WISH, recue um tempo verbal. Nunca use "I wish I know" nem "I wish I would have known".

Aula 05 -- Pre-class

The Vendor Call -- Running International Supply Chain Meetings

Advanced passive voice (it was shipped, it must be renegotiated, it is being applied) + causative have/get something done (we had the contract reviewed, I will get the quote revised). New vocabulary: agenda, quote, renegotiate, SLA, incoterms, customs, tariff, reroute, fulfillment, surcharge, expedite, consignment, action item.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Agenda -- the list of topics planned for a meeting
"Let us follow the agenda so nothing is missed." (Pauta)
Quote -- a formal statement of the price for goods or services
"The supplier sent a quote for the new order." (Orçamento)
Renegotiate -- to discuss an agreement again to change its terms
"We need to renegotiate the contract this quarter." (Renegociar)
SLA -- a contract defining the standard of service promised
"The SLA sets a delivery time of five days." (Acordo de nível de serviço)
Incoterms -- rules that define who pays and who is responsible in shipping
"Under these incoterms, the seller pays the freight." (Termos de comércio internacional)
Customs -- the authority that controls goods crossing a border
"The shipment is still being held at customs." (Alfândega)
Tariff -- a government tax on imported goods
"A new tariff raised the cost of every unit." (Tarifa)
Reroute -- to send a shipment along a different path
"They had to reroute the cargo through another port." (Redirecionar)
Fulfillment -- the whole process of getting an order to the customer
"Faster fulfillment keeps our customers happy." (Atendimento de pedidos)
Surcharge -- an extra charge added on top of the normal price
"A fuel surcharge was added to the freight." (Sobretaxa)
Expedite -- to make a process or shipment happen faster
"We asked the vendor to expedite the order." (Agilizar)
Consignment -- a batch of goods sent together to a customer
"The first consignment arrives next Monday." (Remessa)
Action item -- a specific task assigned to a named owner in a meeting
"Each action item has an owner and a deadline." (Item de ação)

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

Before the vendor call, Klaus sent the agenda. Three points had to be covered. First, the SLA must be renegotiated, because delivery targets keep being missed. Second, the latest consignment was rerouted through Rotterdam, and a surcharge was added to the freight. Third, a new tariff is being applied at customs, so the quote must be revised. To prepare, Fabiana had the numbers checked by finance and got the contract reviewed by legal. On the call, the goods were expedited, every action item was assigned an owner, and the order was fulfilled on time.

1. Which sentence is in the passive voice?
A "Klaus sent the agenda."
B "The consignment was rerouted through Rotterdam."
C "Klaus reviews the contract."
2. What does "Fabiana had the numbers checked by finance" mean?
A She arranged for the finance team to check them.
B She checked the numbers herself.
C The numbers were never checked.
3. Why must the quote be revised?
A Because a new tariff is being applied at customs.
B Because the agenda was too long.
C Because the SLA was cancelled.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Passive & Causative

GRAMMAR

Usado para focar na ação ou para organizar que outra pessoa faça algo. / Used to focus on the action or to arrange for someone else to do something.

Form / FormaMeaning / SentidoExample / Exemplo
be + past participlePassiva: foco na ação / Passive: focus on the actionThe order was fulfilled on time.
modal + be + p.p.Passiva modal: obrigação, regra / Modal passive: rule, obligationThe SLA must be renegotiated.
have + object + p.p.Causativo: organizar que outro faça / Causative: arrange for someone elseWe had the contract reviewed by legal.
get + object + p.p.Causativo informal: conseguir fazer / Informal causative: manage toI will get the quote revised by Friday.

Key point / Ponto-chave: no causativo, a ordem é sempre have/get + a COISA + past participle. Nunca "we had reviewed the contract by legal" (isso é passado perfeito, sentido diferente).

Making Your Case -- Persuasive Language in Negotiations

Cleft sentences for emphasis in supply chain negotiations. New vocabulary: proposal, viable, framework, threshold, commitment, concession, margin, clause, trade-off, counter-offer, stakeholder buy-in, leverage. Expressions: make a compelling case, reach common ground, sweeten the deal.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Proposal -- a formal plan presented for discussion
"I would like to put forward a proposal for the Q4 contract." (Proposta)
Viable -- realistic and capable of working successfully
"This deal is only viable if we commit to minimum volumes." (Viável)
Framework -- a basic structure or set of rules for an agreement
"We need a framework for the twelve-month contract." (Estrutura)
Threshold -- the minimum level that triggers an action
"If volumes fall below the threshold, the discount is void." (Limite mínimo)
Commitment -- a firm promise to do something
"We need a volume commitment before signing." (Compromisso)
Concession -- something you give up to reach an agreement
"We made a concession on price in exchange for faster delivery." (Concessão)
Margin -- the difference between cost and selling price
"Our margin is too thin to offer a bigger discount." (Margem)
Clause -- a specific condition in a contract
"The penalty clause protects us against late delivery." (Cláusula)
Trade-off -- gaining one thing means losing another
"The trade-off is lower price but longer lead time." (Troca)
Counter-offer -- a response to an offer with different terms
"They rejected our price but sent a counter-offer." (Contraproposta)
Stakeholder buy-in -- agreement and support from decision-makers
"We need stakeholder buy-in before finalizing." (Adesão dos interessados)
Leverage -- to use something to maximum advantage
"We can leverage our volume to negotiate better terms." (Alavancar)

It was the freight concession that really got Klaus's attention, not the discount on unit price. The reason this matters is that it gives Bloomberg predictability for supply chain planning. The trade-off was accepting a longer lead time in exchange for a lower threshold. Fabiana also negotiated a revised penalty clause as a key concession. What she recommended next was preparing a formal proposal with exact volume numbers to secure stakeholder buy-in.

C "The freight concession should have got their attention."

A To express regret about the past.
B To emphasize WHY something is important -- giving a clear justification.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Cleft Sentences

GRAMMAR

Cleft sentences DIVIDEM a frase para dar ênfase. / Cleft sentences SPLIT the sentence to add emphasis.

Type / TipoStructure / EstruturaExample / Exemplo

Saying the Unsaid -- Emphasis and Focus in Meetings

Fronting and inversion for emphasis. New vocabulary: scrutiny, transparency, credibility, disconnect, withhold, deflect, acknowledge, scope, maturity, stance, elephant in the room, impact.

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Scrutiny -- close, critical examination of something
"Our team has never faced this level of scrutiny." (Escrutínio)
Transparency -- openness and honesty in communication
"We need radical transparency going forward." (Transparência)
Credibility -- the trust and respect others have for you
"We lost credibility with the Tokyo office." (Credibilidade)
Disconnect -- a gap between things that should be connected
"There was a disconnect between what was promised and delivered." (Desconexão)
Withhold -- to keep back or hide information
"At no point should anyone withhold information." (Reter)
Deflect -- to redirect blame or attention away
"Nobody tried to deflect blame during the meeting." (Desviar)
Acknowledge -- to recognize or admit something is true
"Only after the complaint did we acknowledge the problem." (Reconhecer)
Scope -- the range or extent of something
"Had I known the full scope, I would have acted sooner." (Escopo)
Maturity -- the level of responsibility in an organization
"Not deflecting blame is a sign of maturity." (Maturidade)
Stance -- a publicly stated position on an issue
"Seldom does leadership take such a strong stance." (Posicionamento)
Elephant in the room -- the obvious problem nobody wants to mention
"Let me address the elephant in the room." (O elefante na sala)
Impact -- the effect or influence of an event
"Had we communicated earlier, the impact would have been minimal." (Impacto)

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

The cross-functional meeting was intense. Rarely had the team faced this level of scrutiny. Not only did they miss the Q3 deadline, but they also lost credibility with the Tokyo office. There was a clear disconnect between what was promised and what was delivered. Marcus took a firm stance on transparency: "Under no circumstances should anyone withhold information about delivery risks." Only after the client complained did the team acknowledge the problem. Little did they realize the full scope of the impact. Nobody tried to deflect blame, which showed real maturity. Finally, someone addressed the elephant in the room: the system itself needed to change.

1. What structure does "Rarely had the team faced..." use?
A Fronting with inversion: negative adverb + auxiliary + subject
B Cleft sentence: It was... that...
C Passive voice: was faced by the team
2. What is the effect of putting "Under no circumstances" at the beginning?
A It makes the sentence informal.
B It adds dramatic emphasis and authority to the rule.
C It makes the sentence conditional.
3. What does "Only after the client complained did the team acknowledge" tell us?
A The team waited too long -- they only acted AFTER the complaint.
B The team acted before the complaint.
C The client did not complain.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Fronting and Inversion

GRAMMAR

Quando uma expressão negativa vai para o INÍCIO da frase, sujeito e verbo INVERTEM. / When a negative expression goes to the START, subject and verb INVERT.

Expression / ExpressãoNormalInverted (Emphatic)
Rarely / SeldomWe rarely see this.Rarely do we see this.
Not only... but alsoWe missed + we lost.Not only did we miss, but also...
Under no circumstancesThis should not happen.Under no circumstances should this happen.
Ponto-chaveA inversão cria ÊNFASE dramática. Use em reuniões, apresentações e momentos de liderança.

What Should Have Happened -- Reviewing Supply Chain Failures

Mixed conditionals connecting past and present. New vocabulary: root cause, corrective action, lessons learned, benchmark, defective, inspection, audit, preventive, protocol, rollout, takeaway, flawed.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Root cause -- the fundamental reason behind a problem
"The root cause was a flawed quality control process." (Causa raiz)
Corrective action -- steps taken to fix a problem after it happens
"The corrective action plan was implemented immediately." (Ação corretiva)
Lessons learned -- knowledge gained from analyzing past experiences
"The lessons learned document was shared with all teams." (Lições aprendidas)
Benchmark -- a standard used to measure quality or performance
"We need clearer quality benchmarks for all vendors." (Referência)
Defective -- having a fault that prevents proper function
"The defective units are sitting in our warehouse." (Defeituoso)
Inspection -- a careful examination to check quality
"The defective units should not have passed inspection." (Inspeção)
Audit -- an official examination of records or processes
"We need quarterly vendor audits." (Auditoria)
Preventive -- actions taken to stop a problem before it happens
"The preventive measures include a new checklist." (Preventivo)
Protocol -- a set of official rules or procedures
"We need a revised inspection protocol." (Protocolo)
Rollout -- the process of launching a new system or product
"The APAC terminal rollout had several issues." (Implantação)
Takeaway -- the most important conclusion from a review
"The biggest takeaway is that we need earlier detection." (Conclusão principal)
Flawed -- having a weakness or imperfection
"The vendor's process was fundamentally flawed." (Falho)

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

The APAC terminal rollout failed due to a flawed quality control process. If the vendor had run proper inspections, the defective units would not be sitting in our warehouse right now. The root cause analysis revealed that the protocol was outdated. If our internal audit process were stronger, we would be in a much better position today. The corrective action was effective, but the team agreed that preventive measures are more important. The key takeaway from the lessons learned document is clear: if we had established clearer benchmarks from the start, this situation would not exist today.

1. What type of conditional is "If the vendor had run inspections, the units would not be sitting here now"?
A Third conditional (both clauses about the past)
B Mixed conditional (past condition, present result)
C Second conditional (hypothetical present)
2. What type is "If our audit process were stronger, we would be in a better position"?
A Third conditional
B First conditional
C Second/mixed conditional (present condition, present result with past implication)
3. What is the difference between corrective and preventive actions?
A Corrective = fix AFTER the problem; Preventive = stop BEFORE it happens
B They mean the same thing.
C Corrective = future plans; Preventive = past actions

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Mixed Conditionals

GRAMMAR

Mixed conditionals MISTURAM tempos: passado na condição + presente no resultado (ou vice-versa). / Mixed conditionals MIX tenses: past in the condition + present in the result (or vice versa).

Type / TipoIF clauseResult clause
Past → PresentIf + had + past participlewould/could + base verb (agora)
ExemploIf we had implemented the system, we would not be dealing with errors today.
Present → PastIf + were/waswould have + past participle
Ponto-chaveA palavra "today/now/right now" é a pista de que o resultado é PRESENTE. Se o resultado é sobre o passado, use "would have".

Bloomberg's supply chain has evolved dramatically. Three years ago, the team used to rely entirely on manual tracking spreadsheets. Every Monday, someone would compile the data by hand and email it to the team. The transition to an automated dashboard was challenging. Many people struggled to get used to the new interface. But once they adapted, they became advocates for the new system. The legacy system was eventually phased out completely. The overhaul also changed the mindset: the team used to wait for problems to happen. Now they anticipate them. The entire process has been streamlined and optimized. Today, everyone is used to working with the real-time tools.

1. What structure does "used to rely" use, and what does it mean?
A Past habit that no longer exists -- they relied before but not anymore.
B A repeated future action.
C An ongoing present habit.
2. Why does the text use "would compile" instead of "used to compile"?
A They mean different things.
B Both work for repeated past ACTIONS. "Would" adds a storytelling, nostalgic tone.
C "Would" is more formal than "used to".
3. What is the difference between "get used to" and "be used to"?
A They mean exactly the same thing.
B "Get used to" = the PROCESS of adjusting. "Be used to" = ALREADY adjusted.
C "Get used to" is past, "be used to" is future.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Used to / Would / Get used to

GRAMMAR

Três estruturas para falar de hábitos passados e adaptação. / Three structures for past habits and adaptation.

Structure / EstruturaUse / UsoExample / Exemplo
used to + verbHábito ou estado passado (não mais verdade) / Past habit or stateWe used to rely on spreadsheets.
would + verbAção repetida no passado (só ações, não estados) / Repeated past action onlySomeone would compile the data every Monday.
get used to + -ingProcesso de se acostumar / Adjusting to something newI struggled to get used to the new system.
Ponto-chavewould só para AÇÕES repetidas (compile, send, check). used to para ações E estados (be, have, rely).

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Projection -- an estimate of future outcomes based on data

Accelerate -- to make something happen faster
"If demand grows, we may need to accelerate." (Acelerar)
Forecast (verb) -- to predict future trends based on data
"The demand forecast indicates a twelve percent increase." (Prever)
Milestone -- a significant checkpoint in a project timeline

Deployment -- putting a system into active use

Aula 11 -- Pre-class

Reading the Room -- Relative Clauses in Cross-Cultural Negotiations

Advanced relative clauses (who, which, that, whose, where; defining vs non-defining; reduced). New vocabulary: cross-cultural, high-context culture, low-context culture, save face, read between the lines, etiquette, directness, small talk, reciprocity, common ground, mediator, accommodate.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Cross-cultural -- involving two or more different cultures
"Cross-cultural negotiation requires more than language skills." (Intercultural)
High-context culture -- a culture where meaning is communicated indirectly
"Japan is a high-context culture, which means a lot goes unsaid." (Cultura de alto contexto)
Low-context culture -- a culture where meaning is stated openly and directly
"Germany is a low-context culture, where directness is respected." (Cultura de baixo contexto)
Save face -- to protect someone's dignity in front of others
"Never correct a partner publicly; let them save face." (Salvar as aparências)
Read between the lines -- to understand a hidden or indirect meaning
"When they said maybe, I had to read between the lines." (Ler nas entrelinhas)
Etiquette -- the unwritten rules of polite, correct behavior
"Business etiquette varies enormously between countries." (Etiqueta)
Directness -- being clear, frank, and straightforward
"In some cultures, directness is a sign of respect." (Franqueza / objetividade)
Small talk -- light, informal talk before serious business
"In Brazil, small talk builds the relationship before the deal." (Conversa informal)
Reciprocity -- exchanging favors for mutual benefit
"Reciprocity matters: a concession should be returned." (Reciprocidade)
Common ground -- shared interests both sides can agree on
"We found common ground on delivery timelines first." (Pontos em comum)
Mediator -- a neutral person who helps two sides agree
"The mediator who joined us helped adjust our pace." (Mediador)
Accommodate -- to adjust your behavior to fit another's style
"A good negotiator accommodates the other side's pace." (Acomodar-se / adaptar-se)

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

Cross-cultural negotiation is an art. The manager who leads a meeting in a high-context culture rarely says no directly. A response that sounds like maybe is often a polite refusal, which you have to read between the lines. Silence, which many Westerners find awkward, is actually a sign of careful thinking. The senior manager whose approval the team needs usually speaks last. Etiquette matters enormously here, and the colleague who introduces you sets the tone. In a low-context culture, the buyer who leads the meeting gets straight to the numbers, which can surprise people used to small talk. The negotiator who reads the room, and who accommodates the culture in front of them, is the one who builds common ground. Tokyo, where the first deal was signed, taught the team the value of reciprocity.

1. In "the manager who leads a meeting", what does "who" refer to?
A A person -- "who" is used for people (defining clause).
B A thing -- "who" is used for objects.
C A place -- "who" is used for locations.
2. Why is "which" (not "that") used in "Silence, which many find awkward, ..."?
A Because "silence" is a person.
B It is a non-defining clause (extra info, with commas) -- which is required, never that.
C Because the sentence is in the past.
3. What does "whose" express in "the manager whose approval the team needs"?
A Possession -- the approval belongs to the manager.
B A place where something happens.
C The same as "who is".

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Relative Clauses

GRAMMAR

Pronomes relativos para descrever pessoas, coisas e lugares com precisão. / Relative pronouns to describe people, things, and places with precision.

Pronoun / PronomeUse / UsoExample / Exemplo
who / thatPessoas / PeopleThe manager who leads the call.
which / thatCoisas e ideias / ThingsThe deal that closes.
whosePosse / PossessionThe manager whose approval we need.
where / whenLugares e tempos / Places, timesThe room where terms are agreed.
Non-defining (com vírgulas)Info extra; use which, nunca that / Extra info, never thatSilence, which they find odd, is normal.
Ponto-chaveVírgulas = clause não-definidora (info extra, use which/who). Sem vírgulas = clause definidora (essencial).

The Risk Conversation -- Modals of Probability and Deduction

Modals of probability and deduction (must, can't, may, might, could; be likely / unlikely / bound to). New vocabulary: exposure, mitigate, threat, vulnerability, fallback, buffer, downside, likelihood, hedge, safeguard, off guard, downturn.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Exposure -- the degree to which a business is open to loss
"Our exposure to a single supplier is dangerously high." (Exposição ao risco)
Mitigate -- to reduce the seriousness or impact of a risk
"A two-week buffer helps mitigate shipping delays." (Mitigar / atenuar)
Threat -- a possible danger or source of harm to a plan
"Port congestion is the biggest threat to the launch." (Ameaça)
Vulnerability -- a weak point that could be exploited
"Relying on one factory is a serious vulnerability." (Vulnerabilidade)
Fallback -- an alternative plan used if the first one fails
"We have no fallback if this carrier goes bankrupt." (Plano alternativo)
Buffer -- extra time or stock that absorbs a delay or shock
"We build a two-week buffer into every shipment." (Margem de segurança)
Downside -- the negative side or potential loss of a decision
"The upside is speed; the downside is higher cost." (Lado negativo)
Likelihood -- how probable it is that something will happen
"The likelihood of a port delay is high this quarter." (Probabilidade)
Hedge -- an action taken to reduce financial loss
"Finance will hedge against the currency swing." (Proteção financeira / hedge)
Safeguard -- a measure put in place in advance to prevent harm
"A second supplier is our main safeguard." (Salvaguarda)
Off guard -- unprepared or surprised by an unexpected event
"The sudden price jump caught the team off guard." (Desprevenido)
Downturn -- a decline in business or economic activity
"A market downturn could cut demand by half." (Queda / retração)

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

A good risk review names the uncertainty out loud. Port congestion might ease by Q3, but it could just as easily get worse, so we cannot assume smooth sailing. The exchange rate may move against us, and with thin margins, even a small swing could hurt. When every shipment arrives late, delays must be the main threat -- the evidence is too strong to ignore. A single-supplier model can't be safe; it is far too exposed. A default is unlikely to happen, but the impact would be severe, so it is worth a contingency. And doing nothing is bound to fail. The team that names the downside is the team that can mitigate it.

1. In "delays must be the main threat", what does "must" express?
A A logical deduction -- the speaker is almost certain it is true.
B An obligation -- the delays are required to happen.
C A possibility -- the speaker is unsure.
2. Why is "can't" used in "A single-supplier model can't be safe"?
A It expresses a lack of ability.
B It is a deduction -- the speaker is almost certain it is NOT true (impossible).
C It gives permission.
3. What is the difference between "might ease" and "is bound to fail"?
A "Might" is a possibility; "bound to" is near-certain.
B They mean exactly the same thing.
C "Might" is past; "bound to" is future.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Modals of Probability

GRAMMAR

Modais para expressar o quanto você tem certeza sobre o presente e o futuro. / Modals to express how sure you are about the present and the future.

ModalCerteza / CertaintyExample / Exemplo
mustQuase certo que É verdade (dedução) / Almost certain (true)Delays must be the main threat.
can'tQuase certo que NÃO é (dedução) / Almost certain (false)That can't be our only option.
may / might / couldPossibilidade real / A real possibilityThe rate may move against us.
be likely / bound toProvável / quase certo que ocorre / Probable, near-certainDelays are likely to continue.
Ponto-chaveDepois do modal, use o verbo na FORMA BASE -- sem to e sem -s (might GET, could HURT). / After a modal, use the base verb.

The Decision Meeting -- Reported Speech, Recommending and Reaching Consensus

Reported speech (statements with backshift, reported questions with if/whether, recommend/suggest/propose that + base verb). New vocabulary: consensus, endorse, defer, weigh up, ratify, veto, shortlist, finalize, deadlock, abstain, recommendation, unanimous.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Consensus -- general agreement reached by a whole group
"We are close to consensus on the dual-supplier plan." (Consenso)
Endorse -- to give formal support or approval to a plan
"Which sourcing option do we endorse today?" (Endossar / apoiar)
Defer -- to delay a decision until a later time
"Let us not defer this decision any further." (Adiar)
Weigh up -- to carefully consider and compare two options
"Weigh up the cost against the protection." (Ponderar / avaliar)
Ratify -- to make a decision official by formal approval
"We recommend that the board ratify the top two vendors." (Ratificar / homologar)
Veto -- to formally reject or block a proposal
"Nobody chose to veto the plan." (Vetar)
Shortlist -- a reduced list of the best candidates or options
"Operations drew up a shortlist of three vendors." (Lista final / pré-selecionados)
Finalize -- to complete and confirm something as final
"I will finalize the paperwork by Friday." (Finalizar / concluir)
Deadlock -- a situation where no agreement can be reached
"Let us not leave this room in deadlock." (Impasse)
Abstain -- to choose not to vote on a decision

Recommendation -- a formal suggestion about what should be done
"My recommendation is to ratify the top two vendors." (Recomendação)
Unanimous -- supported by everyone, with no one against
"The vote was almost unanimous, with one abstention." (Unânime)

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

A skilled negotiator never sounds like an order. Instead of "Lower the price," she says the price might be a little high and asks whether there is any wiggle room. Instead of "This clause is wrong," she says she has one or two reservations about it. When a point becomes a sticking point, she does not reject it; she suggests it might be worth revisiting the wording. To ask for a favour, she uses an indirect question: "I was wondering whether you could be flexible on the deadline." Notice that each move adds a modal, a qualifier, or an indirect frame to soften the message and protect the goodwill, so the other side stays amenable.

1. Why does the negotiator say "the price might be a little high" instead of "the price is too high"?
A The modal "might" plus the qualifier "a little" soften the criticism.
B "Might" means she is unsure of the actual price.
C The two sentences mean exactly the same thing.
2. Why use "I was wondering whether you could..." instead of "Can you...?"
A It is grammatically required after a comma.
B The indirect frame makes the request more polite and less pushy.
C It is only used in writing, never in speech.
3. What does "it might be worth revisiting the wording" do?
A It turns a demand into a soft suggestion ("it might be worth + -ing").
B It states that the wording is definitely worthless.
C It is an order to rewrite the clause immediately.

Recurso / MoveComo / HowExample / Exemplo

Qualifiersa little / a bit / slightly / one or two (suavizadores)We have one or two reservations.
Understatementdizer menos do que se quer (not quite / not sure)I am not sure I fully agree.
SuggestingIt might be worth + -ing; I'd suggest + -ingIt might be worth revisiting it.
Ponto-chavePara um pedido educado, use uma pergunta indireta: I was wondering whether... ou Would it be possible to...? em vez do imperativo. / Use an indirect question for a polite request.

Managing Conflict at Work -- Concession & Contrast Clauses

Concession and contrast (although, even though, while, whereas, despite / in spite of, however) for handling disagreement and giving difficult feedback. New vocabulary: friction, grievance, defensive, de-escalate, accountability, candid, empathy, blame, pushback, overstep, assertive, standoff.

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Friction -- ongoing tension or low-level conflict between people
"There is clearly some friction between the two teams." (Atrito)
Grievance -- a formal complaint about unfair treatment
"A couple of people raised a grievance about the delay." (Queixa formal)
Defensive -- reacting to criticism by protecting yourself instead of listening
"He got defensive the moment I raised the deadline." (Na defensiva)

"Our job today is to de-escalate, not to win." (Reduzir a tensão)

"We want accountability for the process, not blame." (Responsabilização)
Candid -- honest and direct, even about hard things, but still kind
"I had to be candid about the impact of the slip." (Franco / sincero)
Empathy -- the ability to understand and share how another person feels
"Lead with empathy before you make your point." (Empatia)
Blame -- saying that someone is responsible for something bad
"Focus on the process, not on blame for the people." (Culpa)
Pushback -- firm resistance or opposition to an idea or decision
"I expected pushback on the new tracking standard." (Resistência)
Overstep -- to go beyond the limits of your role or authority
"I did not want to overstep, so I asked first." (Extrapolar / passar dos limites)

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

Giving difficult feedback is really about acknowledging one thing and countering another in the same breath. A skilled manager never just blames. She says, "Although the deadline slipped, I know you were working with a broken forecast." She concedes the pressure -- "While I understand the workload, the slip still hurt the client" -- and then contrasts two facts: "The cost stayed flat, whereas the lead time doubled." When she wants to keep the goodwill, she leads with the positive: "Despite the friction, your team responded well." Notice that although, even though, while and whereas are followed by a full clause, but despite and in spite of are followed by a noun. Used well, these linkers de-escalate the conflict and turn blame into shared accountability.

1. Why does the manager say "Although the deadline slipped, I know you had a broken forecast"?
A She acknowledges the problem first, then concedes a reason -- it softens the feedback.
B "Although" means she is not sure the deadline really slipped.
C The two clauses contradict each other and cancel out.
2. What is the difference between "despite" and "although" in the text?
A They are interchangeable in every position.
B "Despite" is followed by a noun, while "although" is followed by a full clause.
C "Despite" can only be used at the end of a sentence.
3. What does "whereas" do in "The cost stayed flat, whereas the lead time doubled"?
A It directly contrasts two facts inside one sentence.
B It shows that the two facts caused each other.
C It means "because" -- it gives the reason.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Concession & Contrast

GRAMMAR

Como reconhecer um ponto e contra-argumentar na mesma frase para suavizar uma crítica. / How to acknowledge a point and counter it in the same sentence to soften feedback.

Conector / LinkerO que vem depois / What followsExample / Exemplo
Although / Even thoughuma frase completa (sujeito + verbo) / a full clauseAlthough the team missed the deadline...
Whileuma frase; concede um ponto / a clause, concedes a pointWhile I understand the pressure...
Whereasuma frase; contraste direto de dois fatos / a clause, direct contrastCost stayed flat, whereas lead time doubled.
Despite / In spite ofum SUBSTANTIVO ou -ing (nunca uma frase) / a NOUN or -ingDespite the friction, we agreed.
Ponto-chaveCuidado: Despite the delay (substantivo) e correto, mas Despite the team was late é ERRADO -- use Although the team was late. / Despite + noun, not a clause.

Leading a Project Kick-off -- Future Continuous (will be + -ing)

Future continuous (will be + verb-ing) for describing actions in progress across a project timeline, contrasted with future perfect (will have + past participle). New vocabulary: kick-off, deliverable, work stream, dependency, onboard, ramp up, cadence, scope creep, charter, stakeholder map, ownership, success criteria.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Kick-off -- the first meeting that officially launches a project
"Welcome to the kick-off for the supplier-integration project." (Reunião de abertura)
Deliverable -- a concrete result the project must produce and hand over
"The deliverables for phase one are the charter and the map." (Entregável)
Work stream -- a self-contained part of the project with its own owner and goal
"Each work stream has a single owner."
Dependency -- when one task or stream relies on another before it can start
"The data stream depends on contracts, so watch that dependency." (Dependência)
Onboard -- to bring a new supplier, partner, or member into the system
"We will be onboarding four new suppliers." (Integrar)
Ramp up -- to increase activity or output gradually, step by step
"We will be ramping up the pilot gradually, not all at once." (Acelerar gradualmente)
Cadence -- the regular, predictable rhythm of meetings or check-ins
"I will be running the kick-off cadence personally." (Ritmo / cafência)
Scope creep -- uncontrolled growth in what a project is expected to cover
"Guard against scope creep: new requests go through me." (Expansão descontrolada do escopo)
Charter -- the founding document that defines a project's goal, scope, and owners
"The project charter and the stakeholder map are due by week two."
Stakeholder map -- a view of everyone affected by the project and how much each one cares
"The stakeholder map shows who we will be keeping informed."
Ownership -- being the single person clearly responsible for a result
"Ownership is clear from day one: one owner per stream." (Titularidade / responsabilidade clara)
Success criteria -- the clear, agreed measures that define whether a project succeeded
"The success criteria are on-time onboarding, clean data, zero disruption." (Critérios de sucesso)

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

A strong kick-off is mostly about painting the timeline. Instead of vague promises, a good leader describes what the team will be doing at each point. "Over the next three months, we will be onboarding four suppliers," she says, "and I will be running the cadence for the first weeks." The future continuous -- will be + verb-ing -- shows an action that is in progress at a future moment, not finished. She uses it for the whole rollout: "While we ramp up, I will be tracking the success criteria." For things that are complete by a deadline, she switches to the future perfect: "By the end of week two, we will have delivered the charter." Notice the difference: will be delivering means still in progress, while will have delivered means already done.

1. Why does the leader say "we will be onboarding four suppliers" instead of "we will onboard four suppliers"?
A The future continuous shows the action in progress across the whole period, not as a single event.
B "Will be onboarding" means she is not sure it will happen.
C The two forms mean exactly the same thing in every case.
2. What is the difference between "will be delivering" and "will have delivered"?
A They are interchangeable.
B "Will be delivering" is still in progress; "will have delivered" is already finished by that point.
C "Will have delivered" is a question form.
3. How is the future continuous formed?
A will + be + verb-ing (e.g., will be tracking).
B will + have + past participle.
C will + base verb only.

Forma / FormEstrutura / StructureExample / Exemplo

Ponto-chaveCompare: will be delivering (ainda em andamento) vs will have delivered (já terminado até aquele momento). / In progress vs finished by then.

Disruption Management -- The Subjunctive (It is essential that + base verb)

The subjunctive in formal recommendations (It is essential/critical/imperative that + subject + base verb, e.g., "that the team be notified", "that we escalate", "that the supplier provide") for communicating a crisis to leadership with urgency. New vocabulary: outage, breach, containment, flag up, recovery plan, postmortem, stopgap, severity, notify, brief, fallout, damage control.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Outage -- a period when a system or service stops working
"At two a.m. we had a system outage at the main hub." (Queda / interrupção do sistema)
Breach -- a serious failure or break of security, a contract, or a protocol
"The outage was followed by a data breach in the portal." (Violação)
Containment -- the act of stopping a problem from spreading further
"Containment is in progress, so the failure will not spread." (Contenção)
Flag up -- to raise an issue urgently so a higher level sees it
"I recommend that we flag up any further failure to me directly." (Sinalizar / alertar)
Recovery plan -- a documented set of steps to restore normal operations
"I asked that each supplier provide a written recovery plan." (Plano de recuperação)
Postmortem -- a review held after an incident to learn what went wrong
"We will run a postmortem to find the root issue." (Análise pós-incidente)
Stopgap -- a temporary fix used until a permanent solution is ready
"The team applied a stopgap that keeps orders flowing." (Solução paliativa)
Severity -- how serious or damaging an incident is
"The severity is high, so we treat it as priority one." (Gravidade)
Notify -- to formally inform someone of something
"It is critical that the suppliers be notified within the hour." (Notificar)
Brief -- to give someone the key facts they need, concisely (verb)
"It is essential that leadership be briefed before the market opens." (Informar / dar um briefing)
Fallout -- the negative consequences that follow an incident
"On the fallout side, we should prepare a statement now." (Repercussões / consequências)
Damage control -- actions taken to limit harm to reputation or operations
"For damage control, no one should comment publicly yet." (Controle de danos)

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

When you communicate a crisis to leadership, the language has to sound formal and urgent. English does this with the subjunctive. After triggers like it is essential / critical / imperative, or verbs like recommend, insist, and ask, we add that + a subject + the base form of the verb. Two things change. First, the verb takes no -s, even for he, she, or it: "We ask that each supplier provide a recovery plan" -- not "provides". Second, the verb "be" stays as be, never is or are: "It is essential that leadership be briefed", "It is critical that the team be notified". So in a briefing you might say: "The severity is high. I recommend that we escalate immediately, and it is imperative that no one comment publicly until our statement is ready."

1. After "It is essential that leadership ___ briefed", which word is correct?
A be -- the subjunctive keeps the verb "be" as the base form.
B is -- because leadership is singular.
C are -- because it sounds more formal.
2. Why do we say "We ask that each supplier provide" and not "provides"?
A Because "supplier" is plural.
B The subjunctive uses the base form, so there is no -s even for he/she/it.
C "Provides" is simply a spelling mistake.
3. Which structure triggers the subjunctive?
A It is essential / I recommend / we insist + that + subject + base verb.
B will + be + verb-ing.
C have + past participle.

recommend / suggest / propose+ that + sujeito + verbo baseI recommend that we escalate now.
ask / request / insist+ that + sujeito + verbo baseWe ask that the supplier provide a plan.
Regra 1 / Key 1: sem -she/she/it mantém o verbo base / no -sthat he provide (não provides)
Regra 2 / Key 2: be, não is/areO verbo "be" fica como be: that leadership be briefed (não is/are). / The verb "be" stays as be.

Strategic Proposals -- Complex Noun Phrases (a phased rollout designed to minimize disruption)

Building dense, precise noun phrases that pack information before and after the head noun (pre-modifiers + post-modifying of/from/designed-to phrases, e.g., "a fully costed three-year supplier-consolidation proposal", "the projected savings from the renegotiated freight contracts") -- the language of authoritative written and spoken proposals. New vocabulary: rationale, consolidation, payback period, return on investment, staged approach, cost-benefit, value driver, underpin, compelling, headline figure, quantify, business case.

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Rationale -- the reasons that justify a decision or proposal

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

The language of a strong proposal is dense. Instead of writing a long sentence, English packs information into one complex noun phrase -- a head noun loaded on both sides. Before the head noun we add pre-modifiers: "a fully costed three-year supplier-consolidation proposal". Here proposal is the head noun, and fully costed, three-year, and supplier-consolidation all stack in front of it. After the head noun we add post-modifiers -- usually a prepositional phrase (of, from, in) or a participle phrase (designed to, based on): "the projected savings from the renegotiated freight contracts", "a phased rollout designed to minimize disruption". The head noun is savings and rollout; everything after it modifies it. The result sounds authoritative and precise -- exactly what leadership wants in a business case. So instead of "We have a plan and it will save money and it will take three years", you say: "a three-year consolidation plan with projected savings of four million dollars".

1. In "a fully costed three-year supplier-consolidation proposal", what is the head noun?
A proposal -- the words before it are all pre-modifiers describing it.
B costed -- because it comes first.
C three-year -- because it gives the time.
2. In "the projected savings from the renegotiated freight contracts", which part is the post-modifier?
A the projected -- it comes before the noun.
B from the renegotiated freight contracts -- a prepositional phrase after the head noun "savings".
C savings -- it is the head noun, not a modifier.
3. Why do speakers use complex noun phrases in a proposal?
A To pack precise information densely and sound authoritative.
B To make the sentence longer for no reason.
C To avoid using any nouns at all.

Negotiating Contracts and Terms -- Conditional Variations (Should the supplier miss the deadline, the penalty clause applies)

Bargaining conditionals for precise contract negotiation: inverted forms (Should + base verb for a real condition; Were + subject + to + base for a hypothetical offer) and condition connectors (provided that / as long as / on condition that / unless) -- trading a concession for a condition with professional pushback. New vocabulary: indemnity, bargaining chip, redline, liability cap, default, binding, terminate, waiver, force majeure, amendment, in good faith, penalty clause.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Indemnity -- a promise to cover the other party's losses or damages
"The supplier must give an indemnity against any third-party claim." (Indenização / garantia de ressarcimento)
Bargaining chip -- something you can offer or trade to gain an advantage in a deal
"The faster payment terms are our main bargaining chip." (Moeda de troca / trunfo de negociação)
Redline -- a marked change or objection to the wording of a draft contract
"We sent back the draft with a redline on the penalty wording." (Marcação de objeção / alteração no rascunho)
Liability cap -- a limit on how much one party must pay for damages
"Unless we agree a liability cap of two million per incident, I cannot sign." (Limite de responsabilidade)
Default -- a failure to fulfill a contractual obligation, such as a deadline
"Missing a confirmed deadline counts as a default, and the penalty applies." (Inadimplência / descumprimento)
Binding -- legally enforceable; you must follow it
"The concession must be binding, not just a verbal understanding." (Vinculante / obrigatório)
Terminate -- to end a contract before its natural close
"Either party may terminate on ninety days notice." (Rescindir / encerrar)
Waiver -- a formal voluntary giving up of a right
"The penalty applies in full, with no waiver." (Renúncia / dispensa)
Force majeure -- unforeseeable events that excuse a party from a duty
"The force majeure clause stays standard." (Força maior / caso fortuito)
Amendment -- a formal change made to an existing contract
"I will send the amendment for signature today." (Aditivo / emenda contratual)
In good faith -- honestly and fairly, with sincere intentions
"If they accept those points in good faith, we have a deal." (De boa-fé)
Penalty clause -- a fixed charge for failing to meet a contract term
"Should the supplier miss a deadline, the penalty clause applies." (Cláusula de multa / penalidade)

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

In a contract negotiation, the plain word if often sounds too casual. Formal English offers sharper, more powerful variations. To set a real condition, you can invert with Should: "Should the supplier miss a deadline, the penalty clause applies." Here Should + the supplier + miss (base verb) replaces "If the supplier misses". To make a hypothetical offer, you invert with Were: "Were you to bring the lead time down to ten days, we would halve the penalty." This means "If you brought it down". To attach a strict condition, use provided that, as long as, or on condition that: "We hold the rate provided that you commit to the volume." And unless means "if not": "Unless we agree a liability cap, I cannot sign." Notice: the inverted forms already contain the "if", so you never write "if were you to"; and "unless" already means "if not", so you never write "unless if". When the condition comes first, a comma separates it from the result.

1. "Should the supplier miss a deadline, the penalty applies." This condition is:
A real and formal -- an inverted way of saying "If the supplier misses a deadline".
B a pure hypothesis that will never happen.
C a command telling the supplier what to do.
2. Which sentence is correct?
A "Unless if we get a cap, we cannot sign."
B "Unless we get a cap, we cannot sign." -- "unless" already means "if not".
C "If unless we get a cap, we cannot sign."
3. Why use "Were you to bring the lead time down..." instead of "If you brought..."?
A It is a more formal, hypothetical way to make a conditional offer in a negotiation.
B It means the opposite of "If you brought it down".
C It is only used to talk about the past.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Conditional Variations

GRAMMAR

Como trocar uma concessão por uma condição com precisão formal -- a marca de uma negociação de contrato. / How to trade a concession for a condition with formal precision -- the hallmark of a contract negotiation.

Forma / FormSentido / MeaningExample / Exemplo
Should + sujeito + verbo basese acontecer (real, formal) / if it happensShould the supplier miss a deadline, the penalty applies.
Were + sujeito + to + basese você fizesse (hipotético) / if you didWere you to bring the lead time down, we would halve the penalty.
provided that / as long as / on condition thatsomente se isto for verdade / only if this is trueWe hold the rate provided that you commit to the volume.
unlessse não / a menos que (= if not)Unless we agree a cap, I cannot sign.
Regra / KeyAs formas invertidas já contêm o "if" -- nunca escreva "if were you to" nem "unless if". / The inverted forms already contain "if"; never write "if were you to" or "unless if".

Aula 20 -- Pre-class

End-to-End Communication -- Advanced Discourse Markers (signposting a coherent, extended turn)

Advanced discourse markers for telling the whole story coherently: sequence (to begin with / moving on), contrast (that said / nonetheless), result (consequently / as a result), and summary (to sum up / the upshot is) -- the four moves that hold an extended turn together. New vocabulary: discourse marker, cohesion, signpost, throughline, synthesize, recap, segue, crux, overarching, upshot, standpoint, coherent.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Discourse marker -- a word or phrase that signals the next stage of speech
"Use a discourse marker like 'moving on' to start a new stage." (Marcador discursivo / conector)
Cohesion -- the quality of parts hanging together as a whole
"The cohesion of the talk made it easy to follow." (Coesão)
Signpost -- to mark out the stages so listeners can follow
"Let me signpost where we are going: first the context, then the proposal." (Sinalizar / orientar)
Throughline -- the single idea that runs through the whole story
"The throughline is simple: every decision was underpinned by real figures." (Fio condutor)
Synthesize -- to combine separate parts into one clear whole
"In the recap, I synthesize the whole programme in two sentences." (Sintetizar)
Recap -- a short summary of what was already said
"To finish, a quick recap of the headline figures." (Recapitulação / resumo)
Segue -- a smooth transition from one topic to the next
"That is a natural segue from the negotiation to the results." (Transição suave / gancho)
Crux -- the single most important point of the matter
"The crux of the problem was duplication across eleven suppliers." (Âmago / ponto central)
Overarching -- covering and connecting everything; top-level
"The overarching aim was simple: fewer partners, better rates." (Abrangente / global)
Upshot -- the final result or conclusion that matters
"The upshot is that both sides signed in good faith." (Resultado final / conclusão)
Standpoint -- a particular point of view on a matter
"From a cost standpoint, the consolidation is clearly the right call." (Ponto de vista / ótica)
Coherent -- clear, logical, and easy to follow as a whole
"A coherent story takes them from the problem to the signature without gaps." (Coerente)

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

An extended turn -- presenting a whole programme from problem to result -- only works if it is coherent. The tool that creates that cohesion is the discourse marker: a word or phrase that signals what comes next. There are four key functions. To signpost a new stage, use a sequence marker: "To begin with, the context. Moving on, the proposal." To turn the direction, use a contrast marker: "The savings were clear. That said, the negotiation was tough." (Others: nonetheless, whereas, having said that.) To show an effect, use a result marker: "We held firm on the cap. Consequently, the contract is balanced." (Others: as a result, in light of this.) And to close, use a summary marker: "To sum up, four million in savings." (Others: in essence, the upshot is.) Match the marker to the function -- a contrast marker where you mean a result simply confuses the listener. Used well, these markers give your story a clear throughline from the first word to the final recap.

1. "We held firm on the cap. Consequently, the contract is balanced." What does "Consequently" signal?
A a result -- the balanced contract follows as an effect of holding firm.
B a contrast -- the two ideas push against each other.
C a new, unrelated topic.
2. Which marker best opens a new stage of the story (sequence)?
A "That said," -- this signals a contrast.
B "Moving on," -- this signals the next stage.
C "As a result," -- this signals an effect.
3. Why do speakers use discourse markers in an extended turn?
A To create cohesion and a clear throughline so listeners can follow from start to finish.
B To make the talk longer with no purpose.
C To hide the main point from the audience.

Lesson 21 -- Pre-class

Communicating Under Pressure -- Say Only What You Know

When leadership wants answers now and the facts are not in yet. Key words: holding statement, talking points, preliminary, unconfirmed, speculate, noncommittal, walk back, off the record, buy time, hold the line, composure, level with someone. Structure: distancing language -- it is understood that / is thought to be / is reported to have started / appears to have been.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Holding statement -- a short prepared message you give before all the facts are known
"Let me give you a holding statement now, and a fuller update at four."
Talking points -- the few key messages you plan to repeat in a difficult conversation
"Stick to your talking points: buffer, second supplier, next update."
Preliminary -- early, and not yet final
"These figures are preliminary; the inspection is still running."
Unconfirmed -- not yet checked or officially proven
"There are unconfirmed reports that two pallets were damaged."
Speculate -- to guess about something when you do not have the facts
"I would rather not speculate on the numbers until we have photos."
Noncommittal -- not showing a clear decision, opinion or promise
"They will say your answer sounds noncommittal, so give them a range."
Walk back -- to take back or soften something you said earlier
"Do not walk back what you said about the buffer."
Off the record -- said privately, not to be quoted or used officially
"If someone asks for a number off the record, treat it as on the record."
Buy time -- to delay a decision so that you can get more information
"Promising an update at four buys time without sounding evasive."
Hold the line -- to keep your position when people push you to change it
"When the committee pushes for a date, hold the line."
Composure -- the state of staying calm and in control under stress
"Your composure on the bridge call was noticed."
Level with someone -- to be completely honest and direct with someone
"I will level with you: I do not have a firm date yet."

Stage 1.2: Matching

Practice

Choose the meaning of each word.

Holding statement
Unconfirmed
Noncommittal

Buy time

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text, then answer the questions.

At seven in the morning, Fabiana gets the call: a fire at the contract manufacturer's plant in Penang. By eight, leadership wants answers. She has half of them. So she opens the bridge call with a holding statement, and every sentence tells her listeners where each fact comes from. It is understood that nobody was hurt. The fire is reported to have started in the packaging area. The assembly line appears to have been untouched. The plant is thought to be closed for three days.

None of these sentences says "I know". None of them says "they told me" either. The grammar does the work: it + passive + that, or subject + passive + to. When the event is happening now, she uses to be. When it already happened, she uses to have + past participle: the fire is reported to have started, not to start.

Then comes the pressure. Someone in sales has heard that twenty pallets were destroyed. That figure is unconfirmed, and she would rather not speculate. The committee wants a date; she holds the line and buys time with an update at four. She does not walk back anything she said. And on the parts she controls, she drops the distancing completely: "We have eleven days of buffer. I'll level with you: I don't have a firm date yet." Careful about the facts, firm about the actions.

1. Why does Fabiana say "the fire is reported to have started" and not "the fire is reported to start"?
A Because "start" is an irregular verb.
B Because the fire started before the report: an earlier event takes "to have" + past participle.
C Because the sentence is in the future.
2. What do all the distancing sentences show?
A That the fact comes from someone else and she has not confirmed it herself.
B That she thinks the information is false.
C That she is refusing to answer the question.
3. Where does she stop using distancing language, and why?
A When she talks about the fire, because it is serious.
B When she talks about the pallets, because sales is sure.
C When she talks about what she controls, like the buffer, because those are her own commitments.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Distancing Language

GRAMMAR

Two shapes, one job: the fact comes from someone else, and the grammar says so.

StructureFormExample
It + passive + thatIt is understood / thought / believed / reported + that + full clauseIt is understood that nobody was hurt.
Subject + passive + to (now)is thought / said / expected / believed + to + base verbThe plant is thought to be closed.
Subject + passive + to have (before)is reported / believed + to have + past participleThe fire is reported to have started in packaging.
seem / appearappears / seems + to (have) · It would appear that + clauseThe line appears to have been untouched.
Negativeis not thought to / is not expected toThe line is not thought to be damaged.
QuestionIs it thought that...? · Is X expected to...?Is the plant expected to reopen on Monday?

Never: It is thought the plant to be closed · The fire is reported to start yesterday · It understands that · The line appears being untouched

Lesson 22 -- Pre-class

Influencing Without Authority -- Ask, Don't Tell

Persuading people who do not report to you. Key words: win over, sway, pain point, pre-wire, champion, ally, silo, turf, sounding board, quick win, meet someone halfway, frame. Structure: negative questions and question tags for persuasion -- wouldn't it make sense to...? / isn't the real risk...? / ..., didn't it? / ..., can we?
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Win over -- to persuade someone to support you, often after they disagreed
"She won over the head of Sales in a ten-minute conversation."
Sway -- to influence someone's opinion or decision
"One clear number swayed Finance more than ten slides."
Pain point -- the problem that really hurts a person or a team
"For Sales, the pain point is the delay, not the unit price."
Pre-wire -- to discuss an idea privately with key people before the official meeting
"I pre-wired the proposal with Daniel, so there were no surprises."
Champion -- to publicly support and promote an idea
"Daniel agreed to champion the pilot in front of the vice president."
Ally -- a person on your side who helps you reach a goal
"You need one ally in every team you want to influence."
Silo -- a team that works separately and does not share information with others
"Sales and Supply Chain worked in a silo until Penang."
Turf -- an area of work that someone feels belongs only to them
"Pricing is Finance's turf, so ask before you touch it."
Sounding board -- a person you test your ideas on before you share them widely
"Marcus is my sounding board before any big proposal."
Quick win -- a small success you can get fast, which builds trust for more
"Start with keyboards: it is a quick win, not a revolution."
Meet someone halfway -- to accept part of what the other side wants, so you both agree
"Let's meet halfway: keyboards first, and we review in ninety days."
Frame -- to present an issue from a particular angle
"Frame it as a risk for Sales, not as a cost for Finance."

Stage 1.2: Matching

Practice

Choose the meaning of each word.

Pain point
Pre-wire
Silo
Turf
Meet someone halfway

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text, then answer the questions.

Two weeks after Penang, Fabiana wants a second supplier for keyboards. The problem: nobody in Sales or Finance reports to her. She cannot give an order, so she asks questions that already contain the answer. Wouldn't it make sense to stop depending on one plant? Isn't the real pain point the delay, not the unit price? Penang cost us eleven days, didn't it?

Look at the grammar. A negative question like wouldn't it or isn't does not ask for information: it invites a yes. A question tag does the same at the end of a statement. The tag copies the auxiliary and the tense, and it flips positive and negative: it cost us eleven days, didn't it? / we can't afford another delay, can we? With a falling tone, the tag says: I know you agree.

The questions are only half of it. Before the meeting, she pre-wires the idea with Daniel from Sales Operations and uses Marcus as a sounding board. She frames the proposal as a risk for Sales, not a cost for Finance, and she respects Finance's turf on pricing. Daniel is not easy to win over, so she agrees to meet him halfway: one product line as a quick win. In the end, he becomes her ally and agrees to champion the pilot.

1. Why does Fabiana use questions instead of statements?
A Because she is not sure of the facts.
B Because nobody reports to her, so she invites a yes instead of giving an order.
C Because questions are more formal than statements.
2. Why is it "Penang cost us eleven days, didn't it?" and not "isn't it?"
A Because the verb is in the past, so the tag uses the auxiliary did.
B Because isn't it is only for questions about people.
C Because the sentence is negative.
3. What did Fabiana do before the official meeting?
A She sent an order to Sales and Finance.
B She waited to surprise everyone with the idea.
C She pre-wired the idea with Daniel and tested it with Marcus.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Negative Questions and Question Tags

GRAMMAR

Ask a question that already contains the answer, and let the other person say yes.

JobFormExample
Suggest softlyWouldn't it make sense to...? · Shouldn't we...?Wouldn't it make sense to start small?
Point to what we all knowIsn't it true that...? · Haven't we all seen...?Isn't the real risk the delay?
Tag: positive statementpositive + negative tag (same auxiliary, same tense)Penang cost us eleven days, didn't it?
Tag: negative statementnegative + positive tagWe can't afford another delay, can we?
Intonationfalling tone = you expect agreement · rising tone = you really want to knowIt's the same risk, isn't it? (falling)
Answeringanswer the fact, not the grammarIsn't it expensive? Yes, it is. / No, it isn't.

Never: We lost two days, isn't it? · Wouldn't it makes sense · We can't afford it, can't we? · Shouldn't we to review it?
