Lesson 23 -- Pre-class

Data Storytelling -- The Story Behind the Numbers

Presenting a KPI story to senior leadership. Key words: spike, dip, plateau, baseline, outlier, year over year, slide, bottom out, level off, trajectory, skew, drill down. Structure: narrative tenses -- past simple for the events, past continuous for the background, past perfect for what finished before, and past perfect continuous (had been falling) for a trend that lasted up to a moment in the past.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Spike -- a sudden, short rise in a number
"Freight costs spiked in August, then came back down."
Dip -- a small, short fall in a number
"There was a dip in March, but nothing serious."
Plateau -- a period when a number stays flat after rising
"After eight weeks, the rate reached a plateau at ninety-seven percent."
Baseline -- the normal level you use to compare new results
"The new rate is above our old baseline of ninety-six percent."
Outlier -- a result that is very different from all the others
"June was an outlier: the fire, not the trend."
Year over year -- compared with the same period one year earlier
"Year over year, on-time delivery is up three points."
Slide -- to fall slowly and steadily over time
"The rate had been sliding for two quarters before anyone noticed."
Bottom out -- to reach the lowest point and stop falling
"In June, the rate bottomed out at eighty-four percent."
Level off -- to stop rising or falling and stay at the same level
"The rate climbed for eight weeks and then leveled off."
Trajectory -- the general direction a number is moving in over time
"Tell them the trajectory first, and let the chart confirm it."
Skew -- to distort a result so that it gives the wrong impression
"One freight bill skews the whole quarter."
Drill down -- to look at the detailed data behind a total
"If we drill down, the spike was a one-time cost."

Stage 1.2: Matching

Practice

Choose the meaning of each word.

Spike
Baseline
Outlier
Bottom out
Trajectory
Skew

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text, then answer the questions.

Ninety days after the Monterrey pilot started, Fabiana has ten minutes with the board. She does not read the chart. She tells its story. "Before Penang, our on-time rate had been sliding for two quarters, and nobody had noticed. In June, while we were still relying on one plant, the fire hit and the rate bottomed out at eighty-four percent. By the time the pilot started, clients had been waiting eleven days for keyboards."

Four past tenses, one timeline. The past simple moves the story forward: the fire hit, the rate bottomed out. The past continuous is the background: while we were relying on one plant. The past perfect is something finished before another past moment: by the time the review started, Monterrey had shipped forty thousand keyboards. And the past perfect continuous, had been + -ing, is a process that lasted up to that moment: the rate had been sliding for two quarters.

The words do the rest. June was an outlier. After the pilot, the rate climbed and leveled off at ninety-seven percent, above the old baseline, a gain of three points year over year. Freight had a spike in August, but if you drill down, it was a one-time cost, and one number should not skew the picture. Her advice to herself: tell them the trajectory first, and let the chart confirm it.

1. Why does Fabiana say "the rate had been sliding for two quarters"?
A Because the sliding is still happening now.
B Because it was a process that lasted up to the moment Penang hit.
C Because it happened only once.
2. In "while we were still relying on one plant, the fire hit", which part is the background?
A "while we were still relying on one plant"
B "the fire hit"
C Both parts are background.
3. What does Fabiana do instead of reading the chart?
A She shows more slides.
B She asks the board to read the numbers.
C She tells the trajectory first and lets the chart confirm it.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Narrative Tenses

GRAMMAR

Past simple moves the story forward; the other three tell the listener what was already happening.

TenseJob in the storyExample
Past simplethe main events, in orderThe rate bottomed out in June.
Past continuousthe background: in progress when something happenedCosts spiked while we were moving stock.
Past perfectfinished BEFORE another past momentBy the time the review started, Monterrey had shipped 40,000.
Past perfect continuoushad been + -ing: a process that lasted UP TO another past momentIt had been falling for six months when Penang hit.
Negativehad not been + -ing · had not + past participleWe had not been tracking it weekly.
QuestionHad it been + -ing...? · How long had...?How long had clients been waiting?

Never: The rate has been falling when Penang hit · By then, Monterrey already shipped (use had shipped) · We had been knowing · Clients had been wait

Stage 1.5: Fill in the Blank

Managing Global Relationships -- The Unwritten Rules

Working with New York, Monterrey and Penang across time zones and cultures. Key words: norm, deference, come across as, misread, put someone on the spot, tone-deaf, overlap, asynchronous, handoff, follow the sun, touch base, face time. Structure: be expected to / be supposed to / be meant to -- describing norms and expectations without sounding like a judgment.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Norm -- what most people in a group usually do and expect others to do
"In Penang, a slow reply is the norm, not a sign of trouble."
Deference -- polite respect shown to someone older or more senior
"Greeting the director first is a sign of deference."
Come across as -- to seem to other people in a particular way
"A one-line email can come across as rude in Monterrey."
Misread -- to understand a situation or a signal wrongly
"We misread his silence as agreement."
Put someone on the spot -- to ask someone a hard question in public, without warning
"Don't put Hafiz on the spot in front of his director."
Tone-deaf -- not noticing how your words or timing will make other people feel
"A cost report on their national holiday would be tone-deaf."
Overlap -- the hours when two time zones are both at work
"We only have one hour of overlap with Penang."
Asynchronous -- not happening at the same time; people reply when they can
"Most updates can be asynchronous; save the call for decisions."
Handoff -- the moment one team passes its work to the next team
"The handoff note reaches Penang before their day starts."
Follow the sun -- a way of working where tasks pass between time zones, so the work never stops
"With three sites, we can follow the sun."
Touch base -- to have a short conversation to check how things are
"Let's touch base on Thursday before the forecast goes out."
Face time -- time spent talking with someone directly, on video or in person
"Lucia values face time more than long emails."

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text, then answer the questions.

The board has approved a second supplier, and now Fabiana runs one team across three sites: New York, Monterrey and Penang. Before her first call with Penang, Marcus explains the unwritten rules. "There, new partners are expected to greet the director first. That kind of deference is the norm. And you aren't supposed to put Hafiz on the spot in front of his boss. Touch base with him afterward."

Three structures do the work. Be expected to is a norm that other people count on. Be supposed to is what the rule or the plan says should happen, and in the past it often means it did not happen: the handoff note was supposed to reach Penang by six, but it arrived at nine. Be meant to is the purpose of something: in Monterrey, the Monday call is meant to build trust, not just report numbers. None of them is a personal opinion, so none of them comes across as a judgment.

The clock matters too. There is only one hour of overlap with Penang, so most updates are asynchronous, and the daily handoff lets the three sites follow the sun. Lucia in Monterrey prefers face time to long emails, and a request on Mexico's Independence Day would be tone-deaf. Fabiana's first lesson: never misread a silence as agreement.

A Because it is Marcus's personal opinion.
B Because it is a norm that people in Penang count on.
C Because it happened once, in the past.
2. "The handoff note was supposed to reach Penang by six." What does this tell you?
A It was the plan, but the note did not arrive on time.
B The note arrived early.
C Nobody knows when the note arrives in Penang, before or after six.
3. Why are most updates asynchronous?
A Because Lucia does not like long calls with Penang or New York.
B Because New York asked for it.
C Because there is only one hour of overlap with Penang.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Norms and Expectations

GRAMMAR

These structures describe the rules of the place, not your opinion, so they never sound like a judgment.

StructureWhat it saysExample
be expected toa norm or a duty that other people count onNew partners are expected to greet the director first.
be supposed towhat the rule or the plan says should happenThe note is supposed to reach Penang by six.
be meant tothe purpose or the intention of somethingThe Monday call is meant to build trust.
Negativenot supposed to = not acceptable · not expected to = not necessaryYou aren't supposed to disagree in front of the director.
Pastwas / were supposed to = the plan, but it did not happenThe note was supposed to arrive at six. It came at nine.
QuestionAm I supposed to...? · What are we expected to...?Who am I expected to address first?

Never: You are suppose to · They are expected greet · The note supposed to reach Penang (no be) · It is meant to building trust

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text, then answer the questions.

On Monday, Fabiana presents the supplier update at the quarterly business review. She has five minutes, and then the leadership team asks questions for ten. It is called the rapid round, and it is meant to show how well a presenter can think on their feet. On Friday, Marcus runs a practice round and throws her a curveball: "Why don't we just drop Penang?"

Fabiana does not learn anything new for this. She chooses tools she already has. To tell the backstory, she says that Penang had been running at full capacity when the fire hit. To report news she cannot confirm, she says it is thought that the new line will be ready by November. To persuade, she asks: "Wouldn't one supplier leave us exposed again?" And to sound in control, she says: "Should the CFO ask for a number I don't have, I'll circle back by Friday."

Her rules for Monday are simple. Get to the point in the first sentence. Keep every answer concise, never rambling. If a question is unclear, rephrase it. If it goes the wrong way, pivot. A short hesitation is fine, and if she loses her train of thought, she goes back to the number.

A To give an opinion about Penang.
B To talk about the future.
C To tell the backstory: what was going on before the fire.

B Because she cannot confirm the news yet.
C Because she does not care about the date.

A How well a presenter can think on their feet.
B How many slides a presenter can prepare before the talk.
C How long a presenter can talk.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- The B2 Toolkit

GRAMMAR

No new grammar today. Fluency means choosing the right structure for the job, fast.

The jobThe toolExample
Report news you cannot confirmit is thought that / is reported toIt is thought that the line will be ready by November.
Persuade without pushingWouldn't / Isn't / Don't + subject + verb?Wouldn't one supplier leave us exposed?
Tell the backstoryhad been + -ingPenang had been running at full capacity when the fire hit.
Name a plan that did not happenwas / were supposed to + base verbThe shipment was supposed to arrive on Monday.
Sound in control of a possible futureShould + subject + base verb, ...Should the port close again, we will reroute.
Question formIs it thought that...? · Hadn't they been...?Is it thought that the line will be ready?

Never: It is thought the line will ready · Wouldn't one supplier leaves us · They had been run · The shipment supposed to arrive · Should the port closes

Preparing a five-minute talk for three hundred people at the global operations town hall. (comparative correlatives) -- stating strong conclusions that sound like a leader.

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Gravitas -- a serious, calm authority that makes people respect you

"Even when the video froze, she kept her poise."
Command the room -- to hold the attention of everyone who is listening

Filler words -- words like um, like and you know that add nothing to a message

Resonate -- to feel meaningful and important to the people listening
"A real story will resonate more than a chart."

"That line is a soundbite people will quote."

Pause for effect -- to stop speaking for a moment to make a point stronger
"After the first line, pause for effect."
Land -- to be understood and remembered in the way you wanted (a message or a point)

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text, then answer the questions.

The board approved the dual-supplier contract, and now Priya wants Fabiana on a bigger stage: five minutes at the global operations town hall, in front of about three hundred people. Marcus helps her rehearse. Her hook is simple: last July, a fire in Penang stopped the keyboard supply for twelve days. Then she will pause for effect and let it land.

Her key line is a conclusion: "The longer we depended on one supplier, the bigger the risk became." The structure has two parts, and each part starts with the and a comparative. When the first part changes, the second changes too. It works in the present ("The more connected we are, the more fragile we become") and in a short form with no verb: "The sooner, the better."

Marcus has three notes. Watch the filler words. Use the rule of three for the close. And say the call to action with conviction: "The sooner every team maps its suppliers, the safer we all are." A talk like that will resonate, and a line like that becomes a soundbite.

B the + comparative, then the + comparative.

A It is a question.
B It is in the past, like the sentence before.
C It is the short form, with no verb.

B A long list of numbers.
C A joke.

GRAMMAR

Two things change together. The sentence sounds like a conclusion, so it sounds like a leader.

StructureWhat it saysExample
the + comparative, the + comparativetwo things change togetherThe longer we wait, the higher the cost.
the more / the less + clausemore or less of an actionThe more we rehearse, the less we worry.
Long adjectivesthe more + adjectiveThe more connected we are, the more fragile we become.
Negative directionthe less / the fewerThe fewer filler words, the stronger the message.
Short formno verbThe sooner, the better.
Questionthe structure stays the same inside a questionIs it true that the longer we wait, the more it costs?

Never: More we wait, more it costs · The more faster we move · The sooner, better · the most confident (in the second part)

Navigating Ambiguity -- What They Really Mean

Reading the subtext of three messages after the town hall, from Penang, Monterrey and the CFO's office. Key words: subtext, implication, vague, ambiguous, lukewarm, euphemism, mixed signals, take at face value, read into, gloss over, hint at, loaded question. Structure: substitution with so and not in short replies (I think so, I hope not, I suppose so, I'm afraid not).
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Subtext -- the real meaning under the words that someone actually says
"The subtext of his email was: we will be late."
Implication -- something that is suggested but not said directly
"The implication was that the budget is closed."
Vague -- not clear, with no details
"'Sometime next quarter' is a vague answer."
Ambiguous -- possible to understand in more than one way
"'We will review it' is ambiguous: yes, no, or maybe."
Lukewarm -- showing only a little interest or support, not real enthusiasm
"The CFO gave the proposal a lukewarm reply."
Euphemism -- a soft word used instead of a word that sounds too direct or unpleasant
"'A little optimistic' is a euphemism for 'impossible'."
Mixed signals -- messages that seem to say two opposite things at the same time
"Lucia is sending mixed signals about October."
Take at face value -- to accept something as true exactly as it is said, without looking for another meaning
"Do not take "we will do our best" at face value."
Read into -- to find a meaning in something, sometimes more than is really there
"Don't read too much into one short email."
Gloss over -- to mention a problem quickly so that people do not notice it
"His update glossed over the quality issue."
Hint at -- to suggest something in an indirect way
"Hafiz hinted at a delay without saying the word."
Loaded question -- a question that already contains an opinion or a trap
"'Why is supply chain always late?' is a loaded question."

Stage 1.2: Matching

Practice

Choose the meaning of each word.

Subtext
Vague
Lukewarm
Euphemism
Mixed signals
Gloss over

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text, then answer the questions.

After the town hall, three messages arrive, and none of them says yes or no. Hafiz writes that his team "will do their best" to meet the November date. Fabiana asks Marcus if that is good news. "I'm afraid not," he says. "Don't take it at face value. The subtext is: we will be late."

Short answers like these replace a whole sentence. So replaces a positive clause, and not replaces a negative one: "Will the CFO change his mind?" "I don't think so." Each answer also shows how sure you are. "I think so" is probably yes. "I hope so" means you want it but you are not sure. "I suppose so" is a reluctant yes. "I'm afraid not" is bad news, said politely.

The CFO's office sends a lukewarm email: the proposal has "interesting points" and may need "revisiting" in due course. That is a euphemism for "not now". Lucia sends mixed signals about October, and Hafiz glossed over the quality tests. Fabiana's rule: do not read too much into one message, but never ignore a pattern.

1. What does Marcus mean when he says "I'm afraid not"?
A Yes, and he is really happy about it.
B No, and he is saying it politely.
C He does not know.
2. What is the difference between "I think so" and "I suppose so"?
A They mean exactly the same thing, so you can use either one in a meeting.
B "I suppose so" is a strong no.
C "I think so" is probably yes; "I suppose so" is a reluctant yes.

C Next week, for sure.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- So and Not in Short Replies

GRAMMAR

So replaces a positive clause, not replaces a negative one. The verb you choose shows how sure you are.

AnswerWhat it really saysExample
I think so / I expect soprobably yesWill it arrive on Friday? — I think so.
I hope so / I hope notI want it, but I am not sureWill Hafiz be late? — I hope not.
I suppose so / I guess soa reluctant yesCan we accept it? — I suppose so.
I'm afraid not / I'm afraid sobad news, said politelyIs it approved? — I'm afraid not.
Negative: I don't think sothe natural way to say probably notWill he agree? — I don't think so.
Question: Do you think so?asking how sure someone isThe board will say yes. — Do you think so?

Never: I think yes · I hope no · I don't think yes · I'm afraid no · I suppose yes

Resilience in Communication -- The Polite No

Handling pushback from an angry VP of Sales and a CFO who interrupts, without losing the relationship. Key words: heated, vent, rattled, take it personally, back down, non-negotiable, stand your ground, keep a cool head, hear someone out, validate, reframe, bounce back. Structure: would rather + past and it's time + past -- firm, polite requests and refusals (I'd rather we didn't..., It's time we agreed...).
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Heated -- full of anger or strong emotion (a discussion or a call)
"The call with Greg got heated very quickly."
Vent -- to express anger or frustration so that you feel better
"Let him vent for a minute before you answer."
Rattled -- nervous and upset, so you lose your calm
"The interruptions left her a little rattled."
Take it personally -- to feel attacked when a comment is really about work
"He is angry with the customer, so don't take it personally."
Back down -- to stop insisting and accept what the other person wants
"Greg will not back down easily."
Non-negotiable -- impossible to change or discuss
"The maintenance window is non-negotiable."
Stand your ground -- to keep your position when other people try to make you change it
"Stay polite, but stand your ground on the date."
Keep a cool head -- to stay calm and think clearly in a difficult situation
"She kept a cool head when the CFO raised his voice."
Hear someone out -- to listen to someone until they have finished, without interrupting
"Hear him out first, then give your answer."
Validate -- to show that you understand why someone feels the way they do
"Validate the pressure he is under before you say no."
Reframe -- to present a situation in a different way so people see it differently
"She reframed the budget as insurance, not a cost."
Bounce back -- to recover quickly after a difficult moment
"After a heated call, bounce back before the next meeting."

Stage 1.2: Matching

Practice

Choose the meaning of each word.

Heated
Rattled
Non-negotiable
Stand your ground
Validate

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text, then answer the questions.

Greg Walsh, the VP of Sales, calls Fabiana. He promised the Chicago order for the fourteenth, and the call gets heated. Fabiana feels a little rattled, so she asks Marcus for help. His advice: hear him out, validate the pressure he is under, and stand your ground on the date. "And don't take it personally," he says.

Fabiana prepares two sentences. "I'd rather we didn't promise the fourteenth." "It's time we agreed on a date we can keep." The verbs look like the past, but the meaning is now. After would rather + another person, and after it's time, English uses the past form to make a firm request sound polite. For her own preference, she uses the base verb: "I'd rather wait until Friday."

The same week, the CFO interrupts her twice and calls the budget a luxury. She keeps a cool head, does not apologize, and reframes it: not a cost, but insurance. Greg does not back down at first, but the twenty-first is non-negotiable, and by the end of the week both conversations end with a plan.

1. "I'd rather we didn't promise the fourteenth." Is this sentence about the past?
A Yes, it describes something that happened.
B No, it is a polite no about now.
C It is a question.
2. What does Marcus tell Fabiana to do first on the call with Greg?
A Interrupt him.
B Agree with the fourteenth.
C Hear him out.
3. How does Fabiana respond when the CFO calls the budget a luxury?
A She keeps a cool head and reframes it as insurance.
B She apologizes to the CFO and stops talking about the budget.
C She gets angry.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Would Rather and It's Time

GRAMMAR

The verb is in the past form, but the meaning is now. The past form adds distance, so a firm request sounds polite.

StructureWhat it saysExample
would rather + someone + pastwhat you prefer another person to doI'd rather you sent it in writing.
Negative: would rather + someone + didn'ta polite noI'd rather we didn't promise the fourteenth.
would rather + base verbyour own preferenceI'd rather wait until Friday.
it's (high) time + someone + pastsomething should already be happeningIt's time we agreed on a date.
Questionasking about someone's preferenceWould you rather we waited until Friday?
Rememberno to after rather; past form after the subjectI'd rather wait · I'd rather you waited

Never: I'd rather you send · I'd rather we don't · It's time we agree · I'd rather to wait

Lesson 29 -- Pre-class

The Full Picture -- A Crisis Day

A typhoon closes the port of Kaohsiung and twelve thousand panels for Monterrey are stuck. One day, three moments: the status update, the call with the supplier, and the presentation to leadership. Key words: triage, ripple effect, worst-case scenario, single point of failure, war room, all hands on deck, status update, workaround, round-the-clock, get ahead of, paper trail, debrief. Structures: the crisis toolkit -- recommend that + base verb, should have + past participle, have something done, and mixed conditionals.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Triage -- to decide which problems are most urgent and deal with them first
"Triage the open orders before you call anyone."
Ripple effect -- a series of effects that spread out from one event
"The port closure has a ripple effect on three customers."
Worst-case scenario -- the worst result that could realistically happen
"In the worst-case scenario, the port stays closed for ten days."
Single point of failure -- one part of a system that stops everything when it fails
"One port should never be a single point of failure."
War room -- a room or team where people manage a crisis together
"Marcus opens the war room at seven."
All hands on deck -- a situation where everyone has to help
"It is all hands on deck until the panels ship."
Status update -- a short report on where things stand right now
"Send a status update to every stakeholder by nine."
Workaround -- a temporary way to avoid a problem when the normal way is blocked
"Shipping from Taichung is a workaround, not a fix."
Round-the-clock -- all day and all night, without stopping
"The Monterrey team is working round-the-clock."
Get ahead of -- to act early, before a problem becomes bigger
"Call Greg now and get ahead of the bad news."
Paper trail -- written records that show what was decided and when
"Keep a paper trail of every extra cost."
Debrief -- a meeting after an event to discuss what happened and what to learn
"We will hold a debrief when the crisis is over."

Stage 1.2: Matching

Practice

Choose the meaning of each word.

Triage
Ripple effect
Single point of failure
Workaround
Debrief
Round-the-clock

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text, then answer the questions.

Thursday, 6:40 a.m. A typhoon has closed the port of Kaohsiung, and twelve thousand display panels for the Monterrey line are stuck there. Fabiana opens a war room with Marcus and starts with triage: Monterrey needs the panels by Monday, and everything else can wait a week. In the worst-case scenario, the port stays closed for ten days.

Marcus is angry with the supplier. "They should have moved part of the order last week," he says. Fabiana agrees, but blame can wait. She is having the panels moved to the port of Taichung as a workaround, and in her nine o'clock status update she writes: "We recommend that the Chicago order be shipped first."

At four, she presents the full picture to the leadership team. "If we hadn't added Monterrey last year, we would be out of stock today," she says. One port was a single point of failure; now the team wants a second port too. The CFO asks for a paper trail of every cost, and Priya plans a debrief for next week.

1. "We are having the panels moved to Taichung." Who moves the panels?
A Someone else does it for the company.
B Fabiana moves them herself, early in the morning, with Marcus.
C Marcus moves them.
2. "If we hadn't added Monterrey, we would be out of stock today." Is the company out of stock now?
A Yes, the company is out of stock today and cannot ship anything.
B No. They added Monterrey, so they have stock.
C It will be out of stock next year.
3. What does Fabiana do first in the war room?
A She blames the supplier for ignoring the storm warnings last week.
B She calls the CFO.
C She triages the orders.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- The Crisis Toolkit

GRAMMAR

No new grammar: four structures you already know, each one for a different moment of a crisis.

MomentStructureExample
The email: recommendrecommend / suggest / ask that + base verb (no to, no -s)We recommend that the order be shipped first.
The call: what went wrongshould have / could have + past participleThey should have moved the order last week.
The workaround: someone else does ithave + object + past participleWe are having the panels moved.
The presentation: past decision, present resultIf + past perfect, would + base verbIf we hadn't added Monterrey, we would be out of stock.
Questionchecking a past decisionShould we have moved the order last week?
Rememberbase verb after recommend that; participle after should havethat he call · should have called

Never: recommend that the order to be shipped · should have move · we are having moved the panels · if we didn't add Monterrey last year, we would be

Capstone and Celebration -- Your Fluency Milestone

The last lesson of the program: the year-end review with the board, one final rapid round, and a look back at how far you have come. Key words: come a long way, second nature, comfort zone, track record, pay off, proficiency, stretch goal, momentum, brush up on, sharpen, look back on, hit the ground running. Structures: the language of progress -- wish + past perfect, used to / be used to, cleft sentences, the future perfect, and the more..., the more...
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Come a long way -- to make a lot of progress since you started
"You have come a long way since the first lesson."
Second nature -- something you do so often that you do it without thinking
"Presenting in English is second nature now."
Comfort zone -- the situations where you feel safe and nothing is difficult
"Leading the board review took her out of her comfort zone."
Track record -- all the things a person has done in the past, used to judge them
"Her track record this year speaks for itself."
Pay off -- to bring a good result after a lot of effort
"All that practice paid off in the final review."
Proficiency -- a high level of skill in something, such as a language
"Her proficiency in English opened the door to the Asia review."
Stretch goal -- a goal that is difficult but possible if you push yourself
"Leading the Asia review is a stretch goal for next year."
Momentum -- the energy to keep moving forward once you have started
"Don't lose the momentum when the program ends."
Brush up on -- to practice something again so you do not forget it
"Brush up on your numbers before a big meeting."
Sharpen -- to make a skill better and more precise
"Every rapid round sharpened her answers."
Look back on -- to think about something that happened in the past
"When she looks back on the year, the typhoon week stands out."
Hit the ground running -- to start something new quickly and successfully, with no delay
"She wants to hit the ground running on the Asia review."

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text, then answer the questions.

It is the year-end supply chain review, and Fabiana presents the whole year to the board: the fire in Penang, the second supplier in Monterrey, and the typhoon week. When she looks back on the year, she can see that she has come a long way. A year ago she used to read every word on her slides; now she is used to answering questions off the cuff. It is second nature.

After the review, Marcus says her track record speaks for itself. "What helped most was practicing the hard conversations before they happened," she answers. All that practice paid off: Priya wants her to lead the Asia regional review next spring. It is a stretch goal, and Fabiana says, "I wish I had started all this two years ago."

"Better late than never," says Marcus. "The more you do it, the easier it gets." Fabiana makes a plan to keep the momentum: a podcast every week and a recorded presentation every month. "By next December, I will have led my first regional review," she says.

1. "I wish I had started all this two years ago." Did Fabiana start two years ago?
A No. She started later, and she regrets it now.
B Yes, she started two years ago.
C She will start in two years.
2. "Now she is used to answering questions off the cuff." What does this mean?
A She answered questions in the past, but she does not do it anymore.
B She never answers questions.
C It is normal and easy for her now.
3. What does Priya want Fabiana to do next spring?
A Take a long vacation after the year-end review with the board.
B Lead the Asia regional review.
C Train the team in Monterrey.

No new grammar: five structures from the program that help you talk about where you started, what changed, and where you are going.

JobStructureExample
A regret about the pastwish + past perfectI wish I had started earlier.
Then and nowused to + base verb / be used to + -ingI used to read my slides; I'm used to answering questions.
Focus on one ideaWhat + clause + was / isWhat changed most was my confidence.
Finished in the futurewill have + past participleBy December, I will have led a review.
Growing togetherthe + comparative, the + comparativeThe more I practiced, the easier it got.
Questionasking about the futureWill you have finished the plan by March?

Never: I wish I started earlier · I'm used to answer · What changed most it was · I will have lead · the more I practiced, the easiest it got

Tough Talks: Turn Tension into Trust

How to Manage Difficult Stakeholders

Video · TED · The Way We Work
How to lead in a crisis

Tip: compare her three keys with Fabiana's nine o'clock status update. Which one did Fabiana already use?

Under Pressure: How to Communicate Clearly and Timely During a Crisis

How to Fix Broken Supply Chains

The power of believing that you can improve

  • Use leverage and deploy naturally, with the right -ing forms.
  • Past simple with a time marker versus present perfect with since, for, already, yet.
  • Listen to long, dense messages and note who, what, deadline and action.

Stage 1: Fix It

Quiz

Choose the best version. These come from your gaps in this class.

In class you said: "how long the delay will take?" Choose the correct question.
A How long the delay will take?
B How long does the delay will take?
C How long will the delay take?
In class you said: "our team have been conducting vendor performance reviews every quarter". It is a routine. Choose the best sentence.
A Our team conducts vendor reviews every quarter.
B Our team have been conducting vendor reviews every quarter.
C Our team is conduct vendor reviews every quarter.
Which sentence uses deploy correctly?
A We deployed the milestone when the port closed.
B We deployed the delay when the port closed.
C We deployed the backup carrier when the port closed.

Class of 29 June

Your Role at Bloomberg and Routines

Built from your class analysis: your gaps and your study plan.
▼

Your focus from this class

  • Present simple for routines you have now (come, not came).
  • Verb and noun pairs at work: procure and procurement, deploy and deployment.
  • Numbers that sound alike (fifteen, fifty) and the W sound in when, where, what.

Stage 1: Fix It

Quiz

Choose the best version. These come from your gaps in this class.

In class you said: "this is the time that I normally wakes up". Choose the correct sentence.
A This is the time that I normally wake up.
B This is the time that I normally waking up.
C This is the time that I normally woke up every day.
In class you said: "After 5:00 PM when I came back to home, I came back to home." You are describing your routine today. Choose the correct sentence.
A After 5 PM, when I came back to home, I make dinner.
B After 5 PM, when I come home, I make dinner.
C After 5 PM, when I come to home, I make dinner.
In class you said: "In a normal basis, my Mondays used to be a little bit more calm". You mean your Mondays now. Choose the natural sentence.
A On a normal basis, my Mondays are usually a little calmer.
B In a normal basis, my Mondays used to be a little more calm.
C On a normal basis, my Mondays used to be calmer now.
